questions.question: What is prompt engineering and why does it matter for Java teams building LLM features?
questions.title: Prompt Engineering — What It Is and Why Java Teams Need It
questions.direct_answer: **Prompt engineering** is the practice of crafting and structuring the text inputs sent to an LLM so it returns accurate, safe, and useful outputs. For Java teams it matters because LLM behavior is largely determined by the prompt — a vague prompt yields vague outputs, a well-structured one yields structured, predictable ones. Spring AI's `PromptTemplate` and `SystemPromptTemplate` give Java developers a typed, testable way to manage prompt text with variable injection, keeping prompt strings out of ad-hoc concatenation.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands that LLM quality is a function of the prompt, not magic, and knows how Spring AI surfaces prompt management
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Treating prompts as static strings hardcoded in Java — missing variable injection, system vs user role separation, and testability
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the system/user/assistant role model, discuss how PromptTemplate enables A/B testing of prompts, and mention ChatOptions for controlling temperature and max tokens

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Prompt engineering is how you control LLM output quality** — model weights are fixed, the prompt is your lever.
- **`PromptTemplate`** in Spring AI injects variables into prompt strings cleanly — no string concatenation.
- **`SystemPromptTemplate`** sets the system-role message that shapes assistant behavior across all turns.
- **`ChatClient.builder().defaultSystem(...)`** applies a default system instruction to every call through a shared client.
- **`ChatOptions`** controls temperature, max tokens, and stop sequences per call.
- **Test prompts like code** — fixture-based tests that assert on output structure catch regressions before production.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Prompt engineering is designing the text inputs you send to an LLM to get reliable, safe, useful outputs.

For Java teams it matters because the model's weights are fixed — the only knob you control is the prompt. A vague prompt yields vague results. A structured one yields structured, predictable results.

Spring AI gives you three main abstractions:
- `PromptTemplate` — a Mustache-style template with named variables, so you inject context cleanly instead of concatenating strings
- `SystemPromptTemplate` — sets the system-role message that defines assistant persona and behavior
- `ChatClient.builder().defaultSystem(...)` — bakes in a default system instruction for every call through a shared client instance

The practical payoff: prompts become versioned artifacts you can A/B test and unit-test, rather than magic strings buried in service methods.

sections.title: Build the mental model
sections.content:
**Zero-shot**: no examples in the prompt — just the instruction.

Fast and cheap; works for simple tasks the model has seen in training. **Few-shot**: include 2–5 worked examples of input→output pairs.

Dramatically improves format consistency and domain accuracy without fine-tuning. **Chain-of-thought (CoT)**: instruct the model to reason step by step before giving the final answer. Use for multi-step logic, math, or any task where correctness depends on intermediate reasoning. Cost increases with output tokens. For Java teams: zero-shot for simple extraction, few-shot for consistent JSON output, CoT for complex domain reasoning.

beats.text: Prompt engineering is the practice of designing the text you send to an LLM so it returns accurate, safe, and structured output. It's how you make a general-purpose model behave like a domain expert.

LLMs don't have an API with typed parameters. Text in, text out. Without intentional prompt design, you get hallucinations, format drift, and inconsistent tone. Prompt engineering is how you get consistency without retraining.

beats.text: A PromptTemplate with 'Explain {concept} for a Java developer' lets you reuse the same template for virtual threads, records, sealed classes — just swap the variable. No string glue, no escaping bugs.

items: Hardcoding prompt text as string literals — untestable, invisible in code review

Ignoring temperature — a temperature of 1.0 on a JSON-extraction prompt yields creative, broken JSON
No output format instruction — model returns markdown when your parser expects plain text

questions.question: Compare zero-shot, few-shot, and chain-of-thought prompting — when do you use each?
questions.title: Zero-Shot vs Few-Shot vs Chain-of-Thought Prompting — When to Use Each
questions.direct_answer: **Zero-shot**: no examples in the prompt — just the instruction. Fast and cheap; works for simple tasks the model has seen in training. **Few-shot**: include 2–5 worked examples of input→output pairs. Dramatically improves format consistency and domain accuracy without fine-tuning. **Chain-of-thought (CoT)**: instruct the model to reason step by step before giving the final answer. Use for multi-step logic, math, or any task where correctness depends on intermediate reasoning. Cost increases with output tokens. For Java teams: zero-shot for simple extraction, few-shot for consistent JSON output, CoT for complex domain reasoning.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate can pick the right prompting strategy for a given task and understands the cost/quality tradeoff
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Applying CoT everywhere — it's expensive in tokens and adds latency. Zero-shot is fine for simple classification.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention self-consistency CoT (sample multiple reasoning paths, take the majority answer), ReAct (reason + act pattern for tool-using agents), and how few-shot examples in PromptTemplate can be injected via variables

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Zero-shot** is your default for tasks well-represented in the model's training data.
- **Few-shot** is the fastest way to improve output format consistency — show 3 examples, and the model mirrors them.
- **Chain-of-thought** unlocks multi-step reasoning but costs more tokens — use it when correctness depends on intermediate steps.
- Few-shot examples can be injected dynamically via `PromptTemplate` variables to keep them maintainable.
- **Never use CoT for simple extraction** — it wastes tokens and adds latency without benefit.

sections.title: Three Prompting Strategies Side by Side
sections.content:
| Strategy | What You Include | Best For | Cost |
|---|---|---|---|
| Zero-shot | Instruction only | Simple tasks, classification, extraction the model knows well | Lowest |
| Few-shot | Instruction + 2–5 examples | Consistent format, domain-specific tasks, custom JSON schemas | Medium |
| Chain-of-thought | Instruction + 'think step by step' or explicit reasoning steps | Multi-step logic, math, complex domain reasoning | Highest (more output tokens) |

speakable_v2.hook: Picking the wrong prompting strategy is how teams waste tokens and wonder why the model ignores their instructions. The choice is simpler than it looks.

groups.heading: Zero-shot
groups.text: Instruction only. No examples. The model relies on training to get the task. It's fast and cheap — good enough for simple classification or extraction.

groups.heading: Few-shot
groups.text: Instruction plus 2-5 worked examples. The model mirrors the pattern. It'll improve format consistency and domain accuracy without fine-tuning.

groups.heading: Chain-of-thought
groups.text: You ask the model to reason step by step before it answers. Use it when correctness needs multi-step logic.

items: Zero-shot: classification, entity extraction, simple Q&A — tasks the model has seen at scale
Few-shot: custom JSON schemas, domain-specific labels, consistent output format — show the shape you want
Chain-of-thought: multi-step math, policy compliance checks, complex reasoning — correctness requires intermediate steps

paragraphs: Gotcha: don't use chain-of-thought for a simple 'classify as BUG or FEATURE' prompt. You're paying for paragraphs of reasoning to get one word.
In Spring AI, few-shot examples live inside a PromptTemplate variable. You can swap them at runtime for different domains.

speakable_v2.cap: Zero-shot for simple tasks. Few-shot to lock in format. Chain-of-thought when intermediate reasoning matters. Matching strategy to task saves tokens and improves quality.

questions.question: How do you use `PromptTemplate` in Spring AI to inject variables into prompts?
questions.title: Using PromptTemplate in Spring AI for Variable Injection
questions.direct_answer: `PromptTemplate` in Spring AI takes a Mustache-style string with `{variable}` placeholders and a `Map<String, Object>` of values, producing a typed `Prompt` you pass to `ChatModel` or `ChatClient`. `SystemPromptTemplate` does the same for system-role messages. `ChatClient.builder().defaultSystem(...)` sets a fixed system instruction for every call. This approach replaces ad-hoc string concatenation with versioned, testable prompt objects.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate knows Spring AI's prompt API rather than resorting to string concatenation
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Building prompts with String.format() or concatenation — no structure, hard to test, prone to injection if user input isn't sanitized
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show PromptTemplateContext for multi-message prompts, ChatClient fluent API with .user() and .system() calls, and how ChatOptions pins temperature per request

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`PromptTemplate`** uses `{varName}` placeholders — fill them with `Map.of(...)` at call time.
- **`SystemPromptTemplate`** creates a system-role message — sets persona and constraints.
- **`ChatClient.builder().defaultSystem(...)`** applies a fixed system instruction to every call on that client.
- **`ChatOptions`** controls temperature, max tokens, and stop sequences per individual call.
- Template strings belong in resource files or constants — not inline in business logic.
- Always sanitize user-supplied variable values to prevent prompt injection.

seo.metaTitle: Spring AI PromptTemplate — Variable Injection and ChatClient Guide
seo.metaDescription: How to use Spring AI's PromptTemplate, SystemPromptTemplate, and ChatClient to inject variables into prompts cleanly, set system instructions, and control ChatOptions per request.

familiarity_anchors: PromptTemplate uses {varName} placeholders filled by a Map at call time
SystemPromptTemplate sets the system role — persona and constraints
ChatOptions controls temperature and max tokens per request
speakable_v2.standard_example: PromptTemplate('Summarise this exception: {stackTrace}') filled with Map.of('stackTrace', trace) — same template for any exception
speakable_v2.hook: String concatenation for prompts is how teams end up with injection bugs and untestable prompt logic. Spring AI's PromptTemplate fixes that with one small change.

beats.text: PromptTemplate is a Spring AI class that takes a string with {variable} placeholders and a Map of values, producing a typed Prompt object. It's the typed, testable alternative to string concatenation.

Building prompts with String.format() or + operators scatters prompt logic, makes variables invisible in code review, and can allow prompt injection when user input isn't sanitized. PromptTemplate keeps the template in one place and the values separate.

groups.heading: PromptTemplate
groups.text: User-role template with {variables}. Call .create(Map.of(...)) to get a Prompt. Pass the Prompt to chatModel.call(...).

groups.heading: SystemPromptTemplate
groups.text: Same syntax, but produces a system-role message. Use it to set assistant persona separately from the user's question.

groups.heading: ChatClient fluent API
groups.text: ChatClient.builder().defaultSystem(...) bakes in a system instruction. .user(u -> u.text(...).param(...)) injects variables inline without a separate template object.

groups.heading: ChatOptions
groups.text: Attached to a Prompt for per-call control. Set temperature to 0.2 for structured outputs, higher for creative tasks. Set maxTokens to cap costs.

beats.text: PromptTemplate('Summarise this exception: {stackTrace}') is reusable across every exception your app throws. Swap the variable, not the template. Store the template string in a resource file so the team can review prompt changes in pull requests.

items: Sharp edge: if {varName} is missing from the Map, Spring AI throws at call time — validate Map keys match template placeholders before building the Prompt.
Injecting raw user input without sanitization — opens prompt injection where the user hijacks the model's instructions
Putting temperature-sensitive content through a high-temperature ChatOptions — structured JSON extraction needs low temperature
Forgetting to separate system and user roles — mixing them in one PromptTemplate loses the model's role context

speakable_v2.cap: PromptTemplate keeps prompt strings versioned and variables separate. SystemPromptTemplate sets the persona. ChatOptions tunes determinism. Together they replace string glue with testable prompt objects.
